title: ffn-io-sink-and-soft-routing-granularity-analysis
content:
Status: Draft internal investigation notes
Owner: Daniel Kim (eng-serving-runtime)
Contributors: María, Liam, Priya
Goal: Investigate an observed tail-latency and throughput degradation for long-context MoE workloads when soft (token-level) routing granularity is enabled. Focus on an FFN I/O sink hypothesis where FFN weight/activation movement becomes the critical path under mixed expert dispatch patterns (Llama / Mistral / Qwen variants).

TL;DR
- Symptom: 95th/99th token latency spikes and throughput drops on long-context tests (32k-65k) with MoE enabled and soft-routing active.
- Root cause (working hypothesis): FFN layer I/O becomes a bandwidth/serialization sink due to high fanout of small token dispatches and per-token NVLink/PCIe memcpy overheads + kernel launch serialization for sparse expert subsets.
- Repro summary: Reproduced on 8xA100-80GB and 4xH100 setups; worse on NUMA/PCIe topologies with shared PCIe root complexes.
- Short-term mitigations: increase routing aggregation window (coalesce tokens), force expert batching thresholds, apply eager packing for FFN inputs to reduce small memcpy calls.

Background and why this is different from previous notes
- Many earlier notes focus on gating, prefetch, and routing jitter (we have those). This doc isolates the FFN I/O path when routing granularity is intentionally soft (token-level decisions rather than session/chunk-level). Soft routing reduces wasted compute (finer granularity), but it increases the count of small dispatches which stress host->device and device-side memory movement and kernel scheduling.
- We observed that Llama and Qwen variants (with larger FFN fanout) amplify the effect; Mistral's narrower FFN shapes attenuate it but do not eliminate it.

Experiment matrix (representative runs)
- Hardware: 8xA100(80GB) DGX-ish (NVLink mesh), 4xH100 in PCIe chassis (mixed NVLink), single-socket CPU host (AMD EPYC 7513)
- Models: Llama-2-70B (MoE patched), Qwen-14B-MoE variant, Mistral-34B-MoE variant (small FFN multiplier), baseline dense counterparts for control
- Context lengths: 2048, 8192, 32768, 65536 tokens
- Routing modes: hard-routing (session-level), soft-routing (token-level, threshold=0.2), hybrid (soft with coalesce window=8 tokens)
- Metrics: p50/p95/p99 token latency, aggregate throughput (tokens/s), gpu_util, pci_bus_bw (measured with nvml), memcpy counts/bytes, kernel-launch rate (kernels/s), cudaMemcpyAsync stall time (ri-trace), host CPU syscall rates (epoll, futex)

Key observations
1) Memcpy pattern change
- With soft-routing, host->device memcpy call count increased 3-7x depending on the model and context stretch. Many memcpy calls are small (<64KB), which under PCIe (and UVM fallbacks) leads to suboptimal DMA packetization and higher per-call overhead.
- nvprof/ri-trace showed numerous cudaMemcpyAsync completions followed by many tiny kernel launches for FFN microbatches. Kernel launch overhead and stream contention accounted for ~20-35% of added per-token latency in p95 runs.

2) FFN compute idle time due to I/O serialization
- Measured GPU activity heatmaps: idle gaps align with memcpy and kernel serialization windows. Instead of a steady compute pipeline, we see bursty FFN kernel waves separated by ~200-600us gaps when soft-routing is used.
- Aggregate SM utilization dropped 8-15% in affected runs compared to coarse routing with same effective token count.

3) NUMA/PCIe topology sensitivity
- Systems where multiple GPUs share a PCIe root complex and rely on host staging saw worse penalties (H100 PCIe chassis case). NVLink mesh machines hide some cost due to faster peer-to-peer but still show fragmentation overhead when switching active experts across GPUs frequently.

4) Model architecture interaction
- Llama-2 (wider FFN hidden size and larger per-expert weight matrices) suffers more from frequent small dispatches — more bytes to move per expert and larger kernel footprints. Qwen's attention layout and larger embedding interactions also contribute to more cache churn when experts change per token. Mistral's smaller FFN reduces pressure but the pattern remains.

5) Tail effects from mixed expert fanout
- When routing produces a long tail of tokens routed to many different experts (high fanout variance), the number of unique expert weight pages touched per microbatch increases, leading to worse UVM page faults/eviction activity on less-memory machines.

Profiling artifacts and commands used (examples)
- ri-trace (custom) capture: ri-trace --pid <serving> --duration 600 --out /tmp/ri-ffn-io-trace.json
- nvprof / Nsight metrics captured: kernels/s, dram_utilization, achieved_occupancy, pcie_bw, memcpy-size histogram
- simple counters collected via NVML and nvidia-smi polling (1s): GPU %util, FB memory, PCIe rx/tx
- perf on host to capture syscall hotspots: perf record -F 200 -a -g -- sleep 120
- GPU kernel-level heatmap: made by stitching CUPTI timestamps with ri-trace traces

Representative numbers (toy summary from 65k token runs, A100 mesh):
- Coarse routing (session-level): p95 token latency = 110ms, throughput = 42 tok/s, SM util ~76%
- Soft routing: p95 token latency = 175ms, throughput = 29 tok/s, SM util ~62%
- Soft routing + coalesce window=8: p95 = 125ms, throughput = 38 tok/s, SM util ~72%
- Removing UVM fallback (pinned buffers) reduced soft-routing p95 by ~15% on average

Root cause analysis (single-sentence)
- The combination of many small expert dispatches (from token-level routing) and large per-expert FFN weight matrices creates a memory I/O dominated critical path: small host-device memcopies, kernel launch serialization, and device-side memory thrashing together form an FFN I/O sink.

Hypothesized causal chain
soft routing -> more small dispatches -> more small host/device memcpy + higher kernel rate -> (a) PCIe/NVLink bandwidth inefficiency and (b) kernel scheduling overheads -> FFN compute waves separated by idle gaps -> lower effective SM throughput and higher tail latency

Mitigations tried (results)
- Coalesce window (token aggregation): grouping tokens into microbatches of 4-16 tokens reduces memcpy counts and kernel launch rate. Result: big p95 improvement; tradeoff: slightly more wasted compute for tokens that would have been routed differently but still net better latency.
- Threshold gating: raise gating threshold to reduce number of candidates per token. Result: reduces fanout, but can degrade quality if too aggressive.
- Eager packing for FFN inputs: on host, accumulate small payloads until a size threshold then memcpy once. Implementation in serving-runtime: naive pack reduced memcpy count by ~60% and decreased p95 latency ~18%.
- Pinned staging buffers: avoid UVM fallback; significantly improved memcpy latency variance.
- Kernel fusion: fuse FFN kernel pieces to lower kernel launch rate. Proved effective but requires architecture-specific kernels and increases maintenance cost.

Recommended action plan (short/med/long)
- Short (immediate, low-risk):
  - Enable coalesce-window=8 as default for soft-routing in long-context mode (configurable per-customer). Rollout behind feature flag.
  - Add host-side buffer aggregator to amortize small memcpy calls for FFN inputs (micro-optimization).
  - Pin critical staging buffers for MoE requests (avoid UVM)
- Medium (2-6 weeks):
  - Implement dynamic routing service that monitors memcpy/kernels and auto-adjusts coalesce window and gating thresholds per workload.
  - Add trace-level telemetry for memcpy-size histograms and kernel-launch rates to Console dashboards.
- Long (quarter+):
  - Invest in fused FFN kernels for common model variants (Llama/Qwen). Consider partner work with kernel team.
  - Explore device-side token aggregation (move routing coalescing into GPU) to eliminate host-device memcpy amplification.

Open questions / TODOs
- Quality tradeoff: how does coalescing affect per-token routing quality (hallucination/regression)? Need prompt set evals and A/Bs.
- Is there a threshold where soft routing provides net quality benefits that justify cost vs. coarse routing? Build evaluation harness to sweep quality vs cost across models.
- NUMA-aware scheduling: can we prefer experts colocated on same PCIe root to reduce cross-root memory movement? Feasibility: scheduler-level change.
- Persistent expert warm pages: investigate OS/kernel-level pinning to avoid eviction churn for popular experts. Risk: memory pressure on multi-tenant machines.

Action items (owners)
- Daniel: deploy feature flagged coalesce-window=8 to perf stage; measure regression suite (RI-2463).
- María: implement host-side FFN input packer and add memcpy-size histogram telemetry.
- Liam: prototype dynamic coalesce controller (daemon) and integrate basic signal (kernel-rate, memcpy-mean).
- Priya: run quality evals for coalescing on 10 prompt sets (LLM-regress harness) and report delta.

Notes on communicating with product/CS
- Short message to CS: "We identified an I/O packing inefficiency under token-level routing that increases tail latency on long-context MoE workloads; we will enable conservative coalescing by default and monitor quality metrics. Expect improved p95 latency in most customer workloads, but we will run A/Bs with customers that explicitly want token-level routing without coalescing."
- For Product: provide a comparison matrix (cost/latency/quality) across routing modes and coalescing windows.

Appendix: microtrace examples (excerpt)
- ri-trace snippet (timestamps are relative, us):
  1. 0us: recv token batch 64
  2. 120us: decide routing per-token -> 64 small dispatches
  3. 140us-220us: 64 small cudaMemcpyAsync calls (avg 18KB each)
  4. 260us: first FFN kernel launches in a wave (8 kernels), then idle gap 350us
  5. 620us: second wave of FFN kernels after additional memcpy completions

- Good run (coalesced):
  1. 0us: recv token batch 64
  2. 110us: coalesce into 8 microbatches -> 8 cudaMemcpyAsync calls (avg 140KB)
  3. 190us: steady FFN kernel pipeline with minimal idle gaps

Concluding thought
- There is a sweet spot between routing granularity and system-level I/O efficiency. Soft routing gives algorithmic gains but surfaces systems-level bottlenecks (FFN I/O sink). Short-term system mitigations (coalescing, pinned staging buffers, host packers) recover much of the perf while longer-term work (fused kernels, device-side aggregation) would enable finer-grained routing without the I/O penalty.

References and links
